extracted.intended_audience: legislators, lawgivers, and educators responsible for civic education and family/marriage policy
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for civic legislators on regulating marriage, child-rearing, and public education (curriculum, timing, and permissible arts) to produce healthy bodies and virtuous citizens. Includes specific recommendations on ages, curriculum (gymnastics, music, reading, painting), and restrictions on indecency and certain musical instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of bodily care in early life
rubrics_metrics.description: The body necessarily demands our care before the soul; next the appetites for the sake of the mind; the body for the sake of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the not-reasoning part (appetite) precedes reason developmentally (anger, will, desire seen in children early), legislators should prioritise physical health and habits in early policy for children before focusing on intellectual training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative regulation of matrimony (parties and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator ought to consider the parties and their time of life, that they may grow old at the same part of time, and that their bodily powers may not be different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pairings where the man can father children but the woman is too old to bear them, or vice versa; mismatched ages cause continual discords and disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate spacing between parents and children
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought not to be too great an interval of time between them and their parents; neither should the difference in years be too little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large intervals prevent reciprocal benefits (parental protection, child's affection); very small age-differences prevent proper reverence and cause domestic disputes—balance is needed for family economy and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate marriage ages by reproductive periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Since season for the production of children is determined ... for the man till seventy years, and the woman till fifty, the entering into the marriage state, as far as time is concerned, should be regulated by these periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marry within the bounds of expected fertility so parents and children reach life stages at compatible times; also consider season of year (winter often appropriate) and medical/naturalist advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended ideal ages for marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper time for a woman to marry is eighteen, for a man thirty-seven, a little more or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At these ages bodies are in perfection, reproduction will cease at proper times, and children will reach maturity while parents are not yet extremely aged; marrying too young produces small, ill-formed offspring and increased maternal mortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate physical habit for citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: A citizen ought not to have the habit of body of a wrestler ... nor should he be infirm or too much dispirited by misfortunes, but between both these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizens should have a habit of labour, but not of violent labour or labour confined to one object (as a wrestler's). Labour should be appropriate to freemen; women and men share these needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maternal care during pregnancy (diet/exercise/mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Women with child should also take care that their diet is not too sparing, and that they use sufficient exercise ... the mind ought to be kept as tranquil as possible; for ... the child receive much of the disposition of the mother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators can facilitate by public religious observance; ensure pregnant women have adequate nutrition, moderate exercise, and low-stress environments to benefit offspring's body and disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude imperfect or maimed infants from upbringing
rubrics_metrics.description: Let it be a law, that nothing imperfect or maimed shall be brought up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legislative rule to prevent the rearing of severely maimed or imperfect children is asserted (context: civic fitness); no additional mitigation guidance provided in this passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cease childbearing when parents past bodily perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: When the parents are past that age it is better they should have no more [children].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because children born when parents are old tend to be weak in body and mind; bodily perfection lasts until about fifty (or a few years more), after which further childbearing is discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict condemnation of premarital and adulterous intercourse
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to any connection between a man and a woman, or a woman and a man, when either of the parties are betrothed, let it be held in utter detestation on any pretext whatsoever; but should any one be guilty of such a thing after the marriage is consummated, let his infamy be as great as his guilt deserves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative moral strictness: betrothal infidelity is utterly detestable; adultery after consummation should attract severe infamy/punishment proportional to guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infant feeding and early physical conditioning
rubrics_metrics.description: When a child is born it must be supposed that the strength of its body will depend greatly upon the quality of its food ... they feed them chiefly with milk, as being best accommodated to their bodies, but without wine ... useful to enure them to the cold when they are very little ... accustom children to things at first, but by degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diet should be milk-based (no wine), encourage natural motions, guard against limb distortion, accustom children gradually to environmental stresses (cold) and to relevant future activities (e.g., military training) according to age-appropriate progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early childhood (0–5): minimal instruction, active play
rubrics_metrics.description: The next age to this continues till the child is five years old; during which time it is best to teach him nothing at all, not even necessary labour ... he should be accustomed to use so much motion as not to acquire a lazy habit of body; his play also ought to be neither illiberal nor too laborious nor lazy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise free motion and play (moderate), avoid formal labour or instructive tasks that may hinder growth; design play as preparation for later serious activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow disputes and quarrels among boys as exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: They too do wrong who forbid by laws the disputes between boys and their quarrels, for they contribute to increase their growth -- as they are a sort of exercise to the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators should not ban all conflicts among boys; supervised struggles build bodily strength and resilience; the 'struggles of the heart and compression of the spirits give strength.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Home education until age seven and control of companions
rubrics_metrics.description: At this time and till they are seven years old it is necessary that they should be educated at home ... The preceptors also ought to have an eye upon their manner of life, and those with whom they converse; and to take care that they are never in the company of slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children should be raised at home until seven; teachers must monitor lifestyle and companions, prohibit association with slaves to preserve appropriate civic habits and status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban indecent speech, images, and obscene performances from youth
rubrics_metrics.description: It is as much the business of the legislator as anything else, to banish every indecent expression out of the state ... let them never speak nor hear any such thing ... neither sees obscene stories nor pictures ... illegal for young persons to be present either at iambics or comedies before they are arrived at that age when they are allowed to partake of the pleasures of the table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magistrates must remove obscene statues/pictures (save limited deities), forbid speech and exposure to obscene content for youth, punish offenders (disgrace/stripes before age of common meals; treat older offenders as infamous). Delay attendance at certain dramatic performances until appropriate age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as a public/common concern under magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: Education ought to be one and the same in each; and that this should be a common care, and not the individual's ... it is evident, then, that there should be laws concerning education, and that it should be public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state (magistrates) must take charge of education (public system) to shape citizens according to the city's nature and ends, rather than private, individual family schooling practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective of education: useful instruction for freemen, avoid mean arts
rubrics_metrics.description: The first of these should be taught everything useful which will not make those who know it mean. Every work is to be esteemed mean, and every art and every discipline which renders the body, the mind, or the understanding of freemen unfit for the habit and practice of virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach only what is necessary and suitable for freemen; avoid instruction that makes freemen servile or sordid (occupations for gain, arts deforming the body). Liberal arts may be allowed in moderation but not to mastery if that makes a freeman mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core curriculum: reading, gymnastics, music (and painting sometimes)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four things which it is usual to teach children--reading, gymnastic exercises, and music, to which (in the fourth place) some add painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading and painting are useful in life (judging beauties), gymnastics produce courage, and music serves leisure and potential moral formation; these form the backbone of civic education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of music in education (three possible functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is music ... an amusement and refreshment ... productive of virtue ... or an assistant to prudence? ... music naturally gives pleasure ... it is one of the most pleasing things ... it is therefore useful to instruct young persons in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music can be taught for leisure/relaxation, for forming noble dispositions (imitations of manners), and for cultivating judgment; recognise its power to influence anger, mildness, courage, modesty via harmonies and rhythms and select uses accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and balance between bodily training and intellectual instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Boys should be first put under the care of the different masters of the gymnastic arts, both to form their bodies and teach them their exercises ... when they have allotted three years from the time of puberty to other parts of education, they are then of a proper age to submit to labour and a regulated diet; for it is impossible for the mind and body both to labour at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with gymnastic formation in early years, then allocate an initial three-year post-puberty period to other education before imposing strict labour/diet. Avoid simultaneous intense bodily and mental labour as they are mutually inhibiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit violent gymnastic practices in youth
rubrics_metrics.description: During youth it is very proper to go through a course of those [exercises] which are most gentle, omitting that violent diet and those painful exercises which are prescribed as necessary; that they may not prevent the growth of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extremely painful training or diets early on (e.g., harsh wrestling regimens) that stunt growth or harm long-term athletic development; prefer moderate exercises fostering courage without deforming the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music pedagogy: practical learning early to develop judgment, but not professional virtuosity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary that children should be so taught music as to be able to practise it ... it is necessary for them to practise, that they may be judges of the art ... the practical part may be dropped [when older]; let them learn so much as to be able to receive proper pleasure from excellent music and rhythms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach children practical music early so they can judge quality later, but do not train freemen to professional virtuosity that undermines civic duties; practical mastery should be reserved for paid specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude certain instruments and virtuosic pieces from youth instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: They should never be taught to play upon the flute, or any other instrument which requires great skill, as the harp ... the flute is not a moral instrument, but rather one that will inflame the passions ... the player on the flute is prevented from speaking: for which reason our forefathers very properly forbade the use of it to youth and freemen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid instruments and repertory that inflame passions, encourage effeminacy, or prevent speech (flute). Do not teach pieces of extreme technical difficulty or those which are the object of dispute among masters; select modest instruments that cultivate tasteful judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine professional musical performance to paid artists
rubrics_metrics.description: Playing as mastery should be confined to those who are candidates for the prize in that science ... confined to those who are paid for doing it; for it usually gives people sordid notions, for the end they have in view is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freemen should not become professional entertainers; paid artists may pursue mastery, while citizens should learn music to judge and enjoy rather than to perform for gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select harmonies and rhythms according to moral effect
rubrics_metrics.description: We will now determine whether all sorts of [harmony and rhythm] are to be employed in education, or whether some peculiar ones are to be selected ... different harmonies differ from each other so much by nature, that those who hear them are differently affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose musical modes and rhythms that fix desirable dispositions (e.g., Doric for firmness, Phrygian for enthusiasm) and avoid those that produce grief, excessive softness, or inflamed passions; refer to specialist writers for particulars but apply general moral selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of childhood education periods
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two periods into which education ought to be divided, according to the age of the child; the one is from his being seven years of age to the time of puberty; the other from thence till he is one-and-twenty ... it is much better to follow the division of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise the public curriculum around developmental stages: home education to seven, foundational instruction 7→puberty, then higher instruction to 21; follow natural maturation rather than artificial septenary divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of play as imitation of future civic duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The generality of their play should be imitations of what they are afterwards to do seriously ... the rattle of Archytas ... play ought to be neither illiberal nor too laborious nor lazy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design children's play to model later civic roles and skills (imitation), providing constructive motion and learning without overburdening or becoming servile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Youth as spectators of exercises (age ~5–7)
rubrics_metrics.description: When five years are accomplished, the two next may be very properly employed in being spectators of those exercises they will afterwards have to learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between about ages 5–7, children should observe the exercises they will learn later (spectatorship) to prepare them mentally and habituate them to forms of civic practice before active instruction begins at seven.
